stories.headline: South Africa's Lyle Foster joins Dynamo on loan from Burnley
stories.summary: South Africa's Lyle Foster joined the Houston Dynamo on loan from Burnley on Thursday through summer of 2027.
stories.body:
South Africa's Lyle Foster joined the Houston Dynamo FC on loan from Burnley on Thursday through summer of 2027.

Foster, 25, spent the past four seasons with Burnley, making 89 league appearances and scoring 11 goals across Premier League and EFL Championship play.

He helped Burnley earn promotion to the Premier League twice, including winning the 2022-23 Championship title and securing automatic promotion with a second-place finish during the 2024-25 campaign.

"Lyle presents another powerful, mobile forward to our attacking group," Dynamo president of soccer Pat Onstad said in a news release. "He threatens the space behind the back line, links play well and brings the work rate and intensity that we demand without the ball. Lyle's experience in the Premier League and on the international stage will strengthen our group, and we are excited to welcome him to Houston as we prepare for a strong finish to the season."

Foster joined Burnley from K.V.C. Westerlo in January 2023 after helping the side win the Belgian second-division title and earn promotion following the 2021-22 season. He got his start with the Orlando Pirates and then joined AS Monaco in January 2019 before stints with Brugge and Vitória S.C.

Foster has earned 33 senior caps and scored 11 goals for South Africa since making his debut in 2018. He helped Bafana Bafana advance to the knockout stage at the 2026 World Cup for the first time in federation history.

Houston currently sits second in the Western Conference with 39 points and a 12-7-3 (W-L-D) record and they travel to Charlotte FC on Saturday.

stories.headline: Fantasy hockey drafts: Which player should you take with the first pick?
stories.summary: Picking first? Here are the players you should consider with the No. 1 overall pick in fantasy hockey drafts.
stories.body:
Before mining the draft for valuable sleepers, potential overachievers and breakout candidates, first you have to grab the Shohei Ohtani, Jahmyr Gibbs, Taylor Swift, if you will, of the fantasy hockey world. The megastar to drive your team bus by reliably piling up more points on the daily than anyone else.

I can't remember another season where whittling down the list of eligible candidates to go first overall was so clear-cut. While I forced myself to make positive arguments for several other players as a necessary exercise, each member of the following quartet always emerged superior. So, in loose order, here's who to draft if you're fortunate to do so early on.

Please note that each player's strength is assessed within the framework of ESPN's standard H2H points game, in step with the following formula:

Skaters:

Goals = 2 points

Assists = 1 point

Shots and Hits = 0.1 points

Blocked shots and Special-teams points = 0.5 points

More: Sign up today | Rankings | Projections | Which league is right for you?

Nathan MacKinnon, F, Colorado Avalanche
I'll keep this short because his numbers are superlatively sweet. The Colorado center checks all relevant fantasy boxes, most with extra aplomb. Firing on net more often than anyone else for the third straight year, MacKinnon racked up 74 assists and 30 power-play points on 350 shots, while earning a sufficient number of hits and blocked shots to satisfy any demanding fantasy player. In this space last year, I suggested managers draft MacKinnon first overall and "hope he scores closer to 51 [goals] like in 2023-24." Well, he rifled home 53. Only Connor McDavid equaled MacKinnon in averaging 3.2 fantasy points per game in ESPN's standard fantasy league.

So, once more with feeling: Draft him first overall and hope he scores near 53 like last year. A total of 45 or so would also feel digestible enough.

Nikita Kucherov, F, Tampa Bay Lightning

Bit more to say here. A few weeks after securing his arguably overdue second Hart Trophy, the league's ultimate playmaker is once more ready to set the fantasy hockey world alight. No regular skater averaged more points per game (1.71) than Kucherov in 2025-26, not even that fella in Edmonton who flirted with the 140 total points mark. Exceptional terrain the elite winger might've reached himself had he not missed six games.

Never mind Kucherov doesn't fire on net as much as MacKinnon or Connor McDavid or bolster other nonscoring fantasy categories in any significant way. It's all about the production with this guy, and not just assists. In addition to providing 86 helpers this past run, he also has 44 goals to show for 76 contests. All the while delivering his fortunate managers with an average of 3.1 fantasy points/game, sharing rarefied air with only MacKinnon and McDavid in the 3.0-plus club. No reason to believe we're not in for similar numbers in 2026-27.

Plus, the 33-year-old is reliable enough nowadays. Since missing the entire 2020-21 regular season -- before, ahem, winning his second Stanley Cup a few weeks later -- then half a campaign to follow, Kucherov is serving as remarkably durable. There isn't a fantasy manager on the planet who's going to gripe about any player missing only 11 total games through four seasons. Especially when they're banging out 1.68 points/game three calendars running. Oh, and guess who's entering a contract year with the salary cap skyrocketing? Right. Even the fiercest competitors on the planet aren't immune to such extra incentivization. After MacKinnon, the Lightning star is my top fantasy pick.

Justification for selecting Kucherov first overall: His prospective power-play production. Last year's "measly" haul of 37 points with the extra skater falls well short of totals from previous seasons. Then there's the rather significant gap in quality between Tampa Bay's top unit and its second. Projecting that the elite winger sees a lot of time with the man-advantage and positively regresses back to his personal mean -- 50 power-play points through three previous campaigns -- could rationalize picking him first overall.

Macklin Celebrini, F, San Jose Sharks

It's all about the ceiling with this young man. After erupting for 45 goals and 70 assists in his second NHL season and more than holding his own at the Olympics as a teenager, Celebrini is just getting going. Growing up together with teammates Will Smith (21), Michael Misa (19) and Igor Chernyshov (20), the Ted Lindsay Award finalist is expected to take another step forward as a bigger and stronger player, equally if not bettering, his outstanding sophomore numbers. For starters, don't be surprised if he shoots more often on net, eclipsing the 300-shot mark for the first time. Proud of his 200-foot game, Celebrini could also conceivably improve on last year's total of 53 blocked shots. Those half-points add up fast.

The one fantasy concern lies in the goal-scoring department. Owning a 15.7% shooting percentage and, according to Evolving Hockey, an expected goals rate of 35 ixG, the Sharks center found the back of the net 45 times. Bit of a chasm there. Either Celebrini is just that much better, and therefore more accurate (completely plausible), or some good fortune was in play. My point is that this is why some models project Celebrini to bank approximately 40 goals -- and not 50 -- in 2026-27. Still, the lad's potential is too ripe to disregard. I'm grabbing him without hesitation, once McKinnon and Kucherov are off the board.

Justification for selecting Celebrini first overall: The Ivar Stenberg factor. Coach Ryan Warsovsky now has another option to toss alongside Celebrini at even strength and on the power play. Maybe the 2026 second overall draft pick serves as a delightful fit that brings even more out of the burgeoning superstar. If not, Warsofsky has many other talented and maturing options, even with William Eklund gone for Ottawa.

Connor McDavid, F, Edmonton Oilers

I know what you're thinking: What fantasy manager in their right mind would bypass the best player in our known universe with the second or, my goodness, third draft pick in any conventional league. I get the bewilderment, but hear me out. First of all, this teeny slide is less a knock on McDavid himself and more a reflection of the three preceding names and their dynamite potential in 2026-27.

Then there's the Oilers' power play to think about. Leading the league with a success rate of 30.6%, Edmonton's special teams unit will be hard-pressed to replicate that outstanding figure. Which means McDavid can't again count on nearing a tally of 54 points with the extra skater. Of course he makes Edmonton's unit better. Still, another 54-plus is a big ask for a player who has averaged about half a power-play point per game in his career, including the ridiculous Mario Lemieux-esque haul of 71 in 2021-22.

Another fantasy concern is the influence of the new guy behind the bench. Recognized for his commitment to greater defensive accountability and balancing lines and ice time, Mike Babcock isn't a fan of wild, open offensive play. Of course, he's still going to let McDavid cook, but more likely with the gas turned up to eight instead of 10. This is the coach both the megastar center and Leon Draisaitl wanted. While they won't give a lick about reduced personal numbers if it leads to a Cup, fantasy managers should still slightly temper their expectations.

Justification for selecting McDavid first overall: Because he's Connor McDavid, that's why. In the face of each logic-driven and exceptionally rational argument above, he could still magically score 140 points in 84 healthy games.

stories.headline: Song Yadong KO's Umar Nurmagomedov in massive UFC upset
stories.summary: Song Yadong pulled off a massive upset by knocking out heavily favored Umar Nurmagomedov in the men's bantamweight main event of UFC Fight Night in Shanghai.
stories.body:
Song Yadong saved the greatest performance of his career for his home country, knocking out former title challenger Umar Nurmagomedov in the men's bantamweight main event of UFC Fight Night on Saturday in Shanghai.

Song (24-9-1, 1 NC), a nearly 5-1 underdog at DraftKings Sportsbook, dropped Nurmagomedov with a short right hand, drawing a roar from the crowd when the fight was waved off at 1 minute, 48 seconds of Round 2.

"I believe in myself, and my team believed that I would win this fight," Song said through an interpreter. "They told me I would knock this guy out, and I did it."

It was the second straight fight in China for Song and his second straight win by finish. His most recent knockout win had been in 2023.

Song, making his first appearance in Shanghai since his UFC debut at age 19 in 2017, walked out to a hero's welcome.

"Nine years ago, I wanted to show I could walk in this Octagon," he said. "Nine years later, I want to prove I am the best in the world. I am the best Chinese fighter in the world."

The knockout came after Nurmagomedov (20-2) ducked out of the way of a left hand and right into the path of a short right hand, which connected near his right ear and sent him limply to the canvas. Song delivered three finishing shots on the mat before the referee jumped in.

That sent Song running around inside the cage in celebration, where he nearly ran into Nurmagomedov's younger brother and cornerman, PFL lightweight champion Usman Nurmagomedov, who had rushed in to check on his fallen brother. Usman Nurmagomedov appeared to throw an elbow in Song's direction as the elated winner was running past.

Song climbed atop the cage to soak in the fans' cheers before jumping down outside the cage and running into the crowd to get hugs and high-fives from fans.

"Maybe not today, maybe not tomorrow, maybe not next month, but I will be the first male Chinese UFC champion," Song said through the interpreter, with the "male" designation a nod to countrywoman Zhang Weili, a two-time women's champion at strawweight.

Song, who trains in Sacramento, California, switched to English and yelled, "Give me the title shot!"

stories.headline: Blame the coach: Tale of two disastrous seasons
stories.summary: Fairly or unfairly, the spotlight is on the coaches of the Bulldogs and Broncos after two very different but equally awful seasons.
stories.body:
In front of an expectedly dismal crowd, two of the NRL's biggest clubs met for the last game of their miserable 2026 seasons. Those willing to fork out a minimum $45 for a general admission ticket to the cavernous Accor Stadium were treated to a mistake-riddled first half, with the Bulldogs squandering a majority of possession and being a man up for 10 minutes to go to the break locked at 10-10.

The Bulldogs' best passage of play for the entire night came in the 34th minute, with a move they had obviously been saving up for this meaningless occasion. Starting inside the Broncos' 20, the ball was passed from Jake Turpin at dummy-half to Bailey Hayward at first receiver, to Lachie Galvin at halfback to Viliame Kikau, who turned his back to pass to Stephen Crichton at five-eighth who doubled around before cutting out centre Bronson Xerri to find Enari Tuala who crossed in the corner.

The one movement summed up all that has been wrong at the Bulldogs in 2026. Turpin came on to play dummy-half, and instead of replacing Hayward he pushed him to first receiver, a role he was sharing with Jaeman Salmon at the time. This in turn pushed Galvin to second receiver, where he is at his best in the five-eighth position. Crichton and Xerri were then left to fight over the decoy runner role, otherwise you would have two centres on that side of the field. It's a complete mess and only worked on this one occasion, in a move not seen before nor since.

Coach Cameron Ciraldo has tried his best through 2026 to make the most of the players at his disposal. The Bulldogs lack quality spine players, but Ciraldo has compounded the problem by selecting those he does have out of position. On top of that he has them playing a game plan that brings out the worst in all of them.

Hayward is a half playing at dummy-half, he stands up to pass, his passes are looping and often inaccurate and he poses no real run threat. Early in games Ciraldo has him passing to Salmon who then distributes it with the opposition defence all over him.

Salmon has been playing some career-best football of late, but you still wouldn't have him in a list of the 10 best No. 13s in the League. You certainly wouldn't have him anywhere near a list of ball-playing forwards, and yet week after week Ciraldo has him at first receiver for large parts of the game. He consistently manages to kill off any momentum the Bulldogs may have acquired.

At fullback Connor Tracey forms another part of the dysfunctional spine. If everyone played with his heart the Bulldogs would be a better side, but his handling, nerve under the high ball and attacking prowess leave him a long way short of the attacking weapon the good teams have in that position.

Into the second half, the Broncos found some spark, and began carving up a disinterested Bulldogs defence on the back of characteristic errors.

Crichton, easily one of the best centres in the game, has been moved into the halves by Ciraldo. He has clearly floundered, exposing a poor passing and kicking game, while strangling his greatest asset, his ability to cause havoc when running on the edge. As the Bulldogs fell apart in the second half, he threw a 10-metre spiral pass so poorly timed and directed that it fell into the arms of a Broncos defender who very nearly set up another try.

The Bulldogs were being thumped by a team struggling at the bottom of the ladder, a team which had inexplicably plunged from premiers to no-hopers in the space of a year. Where had it all gone wrong for the Broncos?

They had only really lost Selwyn Cobbo at the end of 2025, while adding depth players in Grant Anderson from the Storm and Tom Duffy from the Cowboys. Sure Adam Reynolds and Ben Hunt were a year older, and wearier, but still capable. Reece Walsh had his share of injuries through the season and front-row talisman Payne Haas had thrown a spanner in the works by announcing that he was leaving for the Rabbitohs in 2027. From a roster perspective there weren't any legitimate excuses for such a dramatic fall.

Rumours circulated that coach Michael Maguire had lost the dressing room. Players were muttering that his methods were too hard, the preseason brutal, egos were bruised, players pushed beyond exhaustion. The morale splintered, the belief in what they were being asked to do waned. Which, to any reasonable outsider would seem completely incomprehensible.

Maguire's methods had brought the club its first premiership in 19 years. The players were covered in glory, the city of Brisbane rejoiced, and now it was all too hard? Did they somehow think the Panthers won four straight titles by taking it easier after winning the first one?

Maguire is a proven winner, with a State of Origin series in his one attempt, two NRL premierships and one Super League title to his name. But, the Broncos aren't the only team to ultimately reject Maguire's methods. At the Rabbitohs he went from a peak win percentage in his second season of 72% to a low of 37% in his final year. At the Tigers he squeezed a 45% win rate out of the perennial strugglers, which dipped to 25% in his final year. His first year at the Broncos brought a premiership with a 65% win rate, which plummeted to 31% this year.

Aren't these players well-paid to do what the coach demands of them? Is it the ultimate display of a chasm between generations? A coach from a harder, more straight forward era, pushing a generation less likely to respond to harsh words or sustain a high level of physical exertion for any prolonged period of time. Success for this generation is often measured in the size of the pay packet, and that arrives regardless of results. Not happy with the coach's methods? Back off your effort a fraction and soon enough he'll be the one shown the door.

The Broncos showed that when committed to the cause, they still have the talent to put on plenty of tries and contain an attack as disjointed as the Bulldogs.

With four minutes remaining in the game, and the Broncos leading 35-20, the Bulldogs played the ball five metres out. Hayward picked it up took a step and a half to his right, and by the time he threw his looping pass to Jacob Preston he was already into the defensive line. The ball hit him on the backside and the Broncos dived on it.

It was a moment that encapsulated a frustrating Bulldogs season in a loss to a Broncos team which really let itself and its fans down.
